newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syria urged to speed up economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Syria urged to speed up economic reform.

text.p: A U.N. agency has praised Syria's efforts to reform its economy, encourage investment, and free its trade but said more action was needed to face economic challenges expected to emerge in the next few years.
The United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) said Syria needed to invest over $18 billion by the year 2000 to find jobs for 450,000 people expected to enter the work force.

Other efforts were needed to improve productivity of the private and public sectors and remove or amend laws and regulations that hinder investment, said the study presented at a seminar on the future of Syria's industry this week.

"The last five years proved that the government was serious in its efforts to encourage private investment and provide requirements for its success, but it still needs to speed up its measures to reform the economy," the study said.
It said industrial investment could be improved by amending existing laws, especially one on hard currency. Investment banks and a stock market should also be established.
The government issued a law in 1991 giving incentives to private investment by Syrians, Arabs or foreigners, and issued several regulations to encourage exports.
The investment law attracted over $8 billion which would be invested in over 1,494 projects that would provide 100,000 jobs, economic sources said.
Hard currency regulations were also eased, allowing Syrians to open accounts in hard currency at local banks.
But economic sources say that Law Number 24, which imposes stiff penalties on hard currency dealing, is still the biggest obstacle to investment.

They say the government, which succeeded during the last few years in abolishing several exchange rates for the Syrian pound that are used in financial dealings, would achieve one unified rate by the beginning of 1998.
They pointed out that the encouragement rate of 43.5 pounds to one U.S. dollar is now being applied to over 80 percent of financial dealings. The black market rate is around 50 pounds to a dollar.

The pound's rate should also be freed to reflect the real value at the market. This would pave the way for the flow of Syrian deposits abroad, estimated at billions of dollars, one economic source said.

The UNIDO study referred to positive developments in Syria in the late 1980s that resulted from an increase in oil production from around 190,000 barrels per day (bpd) to over 600,000. Revenues from oil exports stand at around $2 billion per year and constitute over 65 percent of exports.
The study said annual population growth was one of the highest in the world, standing at 3.3 percent.
This means the population, now 13.8 million, was growing by 450,000 a year. Over 73 percent of the population was below the age of 30.
"As a result of the big growth over 200,000 workers are entering the work force every year and the number would increase to 450,000 in 2000," the study said.
"The population growth and its effects constitute the biggest challenge facing the economy."
